questions.q: Why does the forking workflow exist?
options: It's required before anyone can clone a repository
It lets a contributor without write access to a repository still propose changes, by working in their own independent copy
It automatically merges every pull request
It replaces the need for branches entirely
questions.explain: Most repositories don't grant push access to everyone; forking gives a contributor a fully independent copy they do have write access to, from which they can propose changes.

questions.q: What's the key difference between cloning a repository and forking it?
options: They are exactly the same operation
Cloning only works on GitHub; forking works with any Git host
Cloning downloads a local copy of the same remote repo you still can't push to; forking creates a genuinely separate, independent repository on GitHub that you own
Forking deletes the original repository
questions.explain: A clone is just a local copy of an existing remote repo. A fork is a brand-new, independent repository under your account with its own full push access.

questions.q: In a pull request comparing across forks, what does the 'base' refer to?
options: Your fork and the branch holding your proposed commits
The original repository and branch you want your change merged into
A random branch chosen automatically by GitHub
The commit history of your local machine only
questions.explain: Base is the destination: the original repository and branch the maintainers would merge your change into. Head is your fork and branch.

questions.q: What does 'upstream' refer to in the context of a fork?
options: A branch that only exists locally
The original repository your fork was created from
A synonym for your own fork
A GitHub feature that deletes stale forks automatically
questions.explain: Upstream is the term for the original repository you forked from, as distinct from 'origin,' which typically refers to your own fork.

questions.q: Why do you need to add the original repository as an 'upstream' remote and periodically merge from it?
options: Because a fork doesn't automatically stay in sync with changes made to the original repository over time
Because GitHub deletes forks that aren't synced within a week
Because it's required before you can open any pull request
Because forks are read-only until synced
questions.explain: A fork is a snapshot at the time it was created; it won't pick up later changes to the original repo unless you explicitly fetch and merge from an upstream remote.
